entry.title: India needs a trained regulatory cadre to strengthen economic oversight
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India needs a trained regulatory cadre to strengthen economic oversightIndia needs a trained regulatory cadre to strengthen economic oversight

A dedicated regulatory cadre, backed by UPSC-led recruitment and specialised training, can strengthen accountability and expertise across India's statutory regulators.

premium

India needs a specialised regulatory cadre with structured recruitment, training and cross-sector experience to strengthen the quality, accountability and independence of statutory regulators, argues former civil servant K P Krishnan. | Image: Shutt

K P Krishnan6 min read Last Updated : Nov 24 2026 | 10:02 PM ISTOver the past three decades, India’s economic architecture has undergone a quiet yet consequential transformation. We initiated a calibrated shift away from direct government control. In its place, we built an expansive web of statutory regulatory authorities (SRAs). These are bodies created by statute to regulate economic activity. They operate as distinct legal entities at arm’s length from executive government departments. Today, they determine, enforce, and adjudicate binding rules of conduct across sectors that account for roughly two-thirds of India’s gross domestic product. In everyday economic life, the circulars, orders, and adjudications of these regulators shape market behaviour.  The number of core Union-level economic regulators is about 16, rising to 22 if hybrid supervisory and environmental bodies are included. Across India’s states, there are between 104 and 114 active state-level regulatory authorities. India’s total count of independent economic regulators stands at 120 to 136 bodies. Grouping them into thematic clusters reveals how deeply they penetrate commercial activity.  The total personnel footprint of these bodies is between 30,000 and 44,000. Applying a standard rule of thumb yields an estimated 8,200 to 14,700 officers in the management cadre across India’s regulatory state. These are people occupying managerial, supervisory, and technical decision-making roles. They draft subordinate legislation. They interpret statutes. They conduct inspections, run market surveillance, and pass orders that carry the force of law.  This edifice harbours a structural vulnerability. A traditional executive department operates within strict democratic constraints: Separation of powers flows from the basic structure of the Constitution. But a statutory regulator combines legislative, executive, and quasi-judicial functions under one roof. It writes the rules, it monitors compliance, and it adjudicates disputes. This is a profound concentration of state power.  The Indian legal framework has yet to establish the checks and balances required to restrain arbitrary power and achieve state capability within regulatory bodies. When power is concentrated in this manner, the intellectual rigour and grounding in administrative law of regulatory personnel become the primary barrier to state excess. This puts a high burden upon staff quality and training procedures.  Yet, the human resource machinery in these bodies is deficient. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) maintains a quasi-permanent formal recruitment apparatus suited to its large internal hiring scale. Outside the RBI, most regulators rely on ad hoc recruitment and short-term deputation arrangements. For each individual regulator, the annual requirement of managerial personnel is small. The number of officers eligible for internal promotion each year is too small to justify setting up recruitment mechanisms at a commensurate scale. Fragmented, one-off hiring leads to uneven capacity, high reliance on short-term deputations, and inconsistent regulatory quality across sectors and states.  We must see regulation as a distinct skill. Every regulator requires people that combine two domains of knowledge. The first is the knowledge of regulation in an abstract sense. The second is the knowledge of the specific sector. The Securities and Exchange Board of India and the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India do roughly the same things, applied to different domains. We need to cultivate this expertise of regulation in a workforce for India. That skill is best developed when individuals gain work experience across multiple regulatory organisations.  Currently, many organisations develop an obsessive culture of protecting their own turf through thick and thin. The personnel develop a tunnel vision, expecting to work in one place from cradle to grave. This damages the quality of public administration. It would be better if regulation is seen as a career with many possible employers.  Historical precedent offers a useful guide. In the 1950s, India established the Industrial Management Pool (IMP) to build a specialised pool of managerial talent for senior economic roles in government. The IMP was short-lived on account of pressures mounted by the organised civil services. A modern equivalent tailored to statutory regulation is long overdue. It can be done with the cooperation and participation of the organised civil services.  At a future date, India could build an “Indian Regulatory Service” with direct intake after a competitive examination, allowing individuals to work their entire  lives in regulatory bodies. But something more incremental can be done right away. India’s organised civil services house a large body of officers recruited centrally through the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC). They are trained at established institutions and seasoned through years of administrative experience. Can we envision a concept where, after 15 years of service, officers have the choice of applying for a transfer into a new regulatory cadre?  The fact that these individuals have worked in government for 15 years ensures that the foundations of constitutional and administrative law are already in place. This is a vital ingredient for ensuring effective regulation without the excesses of arbitrary power. Building on the idea of an Indian Institute of Regulation, mooted in a recent Economic Survey, selected regulatory service officers could first undergo a structured programme. This should be a six-month to one-year curriculum focused on the domain-agnostic foundations of regulation. They must study the economic analysis of market failures, administrative law, cost-benefit analysis, regulatory impact assessment, and accountability.  Once this training is complete, these individuals could enter regulators based on job openings. There should be a five-year term in any one organisation. This solves the problem of cradle-to-grave tunnel vision.  Just as the IMP sought to balance specialised expertise with administrative continuity, a thoughtfully designed regulatory cadre should preserve a healthy mix of insiders and outsiders. Towards this end, each regulator should have a twin-track system of hiring. The first track brings in personnel focused upon regulation through the centralised cadre. The second track brings in lateral recruitment from markets, academia, and law.  If statutory regulators are to govern two-thirds of the economy with fairness, predictability, and technical authority, staffing them needs to be undertaken with the same rigour, independence and fairness that is associated with the civil service recruitment through the UPSC. Article 321 of the Constitution explicitly provides for this.  A UPSC-enabled, pan-Indian regulatory cadre, anchored in structured training and a balanced mix of talent, would give India’s regulatory state the human capital its responsibilities demand. 
 The writer is an honorary senior fellow at the Isaac Centre for Public Policy at Ashoka University, and a former civil servant   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Union Budget needs seven reforms to unlock infrastructure investment
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Union Budget needs seven reforms to unlock infrastructure investmentUnion Budget needs seven reforms to unlock infrastructure investment

The seven proposals include raising infrastructure spending to ₹14 trillion, prioritising railways, reviving municipal bonds and ring-fencing asset monetisation proceeds.

premium

India needs a stronger infrastructure investment pipeline, better urban financing and greater private sector participation to sustain economic growth, with seven Budget proposals outlining ways to accelerate infrastructure development. | Image: Bloomberg

Vinayak Chatterjee5 min read Last Updated : Nov 24 2026 | 11:46 PM ISTIn India, the Union Budget is not just a statement of national accounts, but also an instrument to direct development efforts. Here are seven recommendations for the infrastructure sector that could help the overall effort.  1. Budget outlay should be around ₹14 trillion: Substantial infrastructure spending must continue to be viewed as the turbocharger for economic growth because of its high multiplier effect. Public expenditure crowds-in private investments too. The table sets out the rationale for this recommendation.  2. Prioritising rail over road: In the 2026-27 Budget, the allocation for the roads sector was ₹2.94 trillion, while that for railways was ₹2.78 trillion. There is a strong case for now emphasising rail over road. The reasons are fourfold: (i) Roads have reached a stage of maturity; (ii) the pace of road construction has slowed down; (iii) the roads sector has been very successful in garnering private capital through InvITs and other monetisation efforts; and (iv) the railways need more financial support for the completion of the Bullet Train project, seven high-speed rail corridors, and a variety of other development expenditures. It is, therefore, recommended that the budget outlay for railways be increased to ₹3.50 trillion, an increase of 25 per cent from last year, while the road budget is maintained at the same level of ₹2.94 trillion.  3. Ramping up the municipal bonds market: Rapid and rampant urbanisation is putting a huge strain on urban financing needs. A key requirement for urban infrastructure development is the ability of urban local bodies (ULBs) to raise funds through municipal bonds. Progress has been shallow. There are 4,979 ULBs, and only ₹4,540 crore has been raised through 31 issuances by 22 municipal corporations since 2017. In the United States, the municipal bond market (Munis) is about $4.2 trillion and has helped meet 75 per cent of US urban infrastructure needs for over 100 years. India’s incentives are ₹13 crore per ₹100 crore (capped at ₹26 crore per ULB) and ₹100 crore for a single issue above ₹1,000 crore. The issues have been small (₹25 crore to ₹224 crore). Over 75 per cent of bond value sits with the top 10 cities. It is recommended that Budget move from subsidising issuances to forcing market readiness and financial credibility — make audited accounts mandatory, insist on credit ratings and standard disclosures as a pre-condition for devolution of funds from the Centre to the state. It would also be worthwhile to restore the tax-exempt status of municipal bond interest, as was the case from 2000-2005.     4. Implementing UMTA: Seamless urban transportation is a mirage. Back-of-the-envelope calculations of “generalised cost of commuting” (i.e. cash costs + travel time cost) indicate that this has now become as high as 15-19 per cent of household budgets. This is a rising stress point for the urban commuter and more worrying than inflation. As far back as 2006, the Ministry of Urban Development released the National Urban Transport Policy, which recommended the creation of a Unified Metropolitan Transport Authority (UMTA), which would be responsible for all forms of urban transport for all cities with a population above 1 million. There is yet no “real” implementation on the ground. The finance ministry, perforce, has to take the lead in solving this, as it also involves pushing a long-pending Constitutional Amendment — the 74th Amendment. The Budget Speech would be a good place to start, with the finance minister announcing the setting up of a high-powered UMTA Implementation Task Force.  5. A group taxation regime for infra SPVs: Any medium-sized private infra player will have 20-30 special purpose vehicles (SPVs) while large players have to contend with over 50 at any point of time. A group taxation regime  allowing firms to “consolidate” profits and losses in its infrastructure Holding Company (HoldCo.) would stabilise cash flows, strengthen credit profiles, and reduce borrowing costs.  6. ‘Monetisation’ proceeds to be ring-fenced: The launch of the National Monetisation Pipeline (NMP 2.0) in February 2026, targeting ₹16.72 trillion (2026-30) is now a key window for getting private capital into the sector, often termed “PPP by the side-door”. Recent reports indicate that FY27 may garner around ₹2.9 trillion. It would be useful to create a ring-fenced “National Infra Development Fund” into which the proceeds of “monetisation” are clearly and visibly channelised and earmarked for fresh infra creation, and not lost in the Consolidated Fund of India.  7. A bigger pool of investible projects for private sector: The binding constraint for private capital is, surprisingly, the absence of an adequate pipeline of fresh, bankable projects that are sufficiently de-risked. Assuming that the implementation cycle of an infra project is four years, we need a “shovel-ready” pipeline of roughly ₹8.4 trillion X 4 years = ₹33.6 trillion in the here-and-now.  This assumes the intent is to raise private capital investment to 30 per cent of gross infrastructure investments. Are there this many “shovel-ready” projects currently in the pipeline? Certainly not! It would thus be useful for the Ministry of Finance, to aggressively push, and monitor this aspect. Alongside, serious reform of PPP (public-private partnership) systems and structures is essential.  These seven suggestions, singly and collectively, could provide an infrastructure-led boost to economic development.

entry.title: The article a CII president will write in 2047: A roadmap for industry
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The article a CII president will write in 2047: A roadmap for industryThe article a CII president will write in 2047: A roadmap for industry

From deeper domestic capabilities to international competitiveness, here are 6 priorities for industry

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

R Mukundan5 min read Last Updated : Nov 24 2026 | 9:29 PM ISTSometime in August 2047, as India marks 100 years of Independence, a president of the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) may write in this newspaper and the article could read something like this:  “India enters its second century of freedom as a developed economy. Average incomes have reached high-income levels, manufacturing contributes a quarter of national output, and Indian companies are global leaders in pharmaceuticals, specialised materials, electronics, semiconductors and clean energy technologies.  Made in India has become synonymous with quality. Indian businesses invest substantially in research, own valuable intellectual property and compete internationally. Most working Indians have formal jobs with rising wages, women’s workforce participation has risen, and small suppliers have become global competitors.  None of this was inevitable. It was built, decision by decision, from the middle of the 2020s.”  That article remains unwritten. The distance between this hypothetical future and where we stand today defines the task before us.  India’s per capita gross national income was $2,760 in 2025, against the World Bank’s high-income threshold of over $14,375. Manufacturing contributes around 15 per cent of gross value added, while research and development (R&D) expenditure is approximately 0.84 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP), less than half from business. Women’s labour force participation remains below men’s. These figures are not a criticism of our progress, but a measure of the transformation still required.  Over the past 12 years, the government has laid strong foundations for this journey. Sustained infrastructure investment, goods and services tax, digital public infrastructure, Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, corporate tax reforms, production linked incentive schemes and trade agreements have strengthened India’s economic capabilities. The Reserve Bank of India and the Securities and Exchange Board of India have contributed to financial stability, deeper capital markets and investor confidence. The consistency of reforms, despite global shocks, has mattered. Equally, continued reform will be necessary as technology, markets and global competition evolve.  The results are visible. Smartphones emerged as India’s largest individual export item in FY26. As many as 12 semiconductor projects have been approved. Non-fossil power capacity crossed 300 gigawatts in July 2026. India’s investment rate reached 34.5 per cent of GDP in FY25, while CII’s Private Investment Barometer records private project announcements of ~26.6 trillion during April-September 2026 — 86 per cent from private firms.  These are considerable achievements, but they represent the foundations of India’s transformation, not its completion. Sustained growth of around 8 per cent over the coming decades will require the government and industry to build on them with greater ambition.  For a CII President in 2047 to write the article imagined above, Indian industry must accomplish six things.  First, invest ahead of demand. The Prime Minister’s call to place India First in long-term investment decisions is particularly relevant. Today’s investment pipeline is encouraging, but the real test is how quickly announcements become productive capacity, and whether they create competitive enterprises.  Second, build depth alongside scale. India manufactures medicines but imports many critical ingredients, assembles electronics with imported components and remains dependent on overseas suppliers for advanced materials. Industry must progressively develop domestic capabilities in design, engineering, technology and higher-value components, competitively rather than through permanent protection.  Third, invest in knowledge. India’s ambitions cannot be realised with present levels of business R&D. Companies must invest more in research, strengthen partnerships with universities, develop indigenous technologies and build globally competitive intellectual property.  Fourth, translate productivity into prosperity. A developed economy requires productive employment and rising wages. Industry must expand apprenticeships, invest in continuous workforce training, create greater opportunities for women and ensure that technological progress benefits workers as well.  Fifth, compete for the world. India’s domestic market of 1.4 billion people must become a platform for global competitiveness, not a shelter from it. Companies must meet international quality standards, use trade agreements effectively and develop products for markets in developed and emerging economies.  Sixth, take smaller enterprises along. Large companies must strengthen supplier ecosystems through technology partnerships, quality certification, predictable procurement and timely payments. India’s industrial competitiveness will ultimately depend on the capabilities of thousands of MSMEs, not only its largest companies.  None of these tasks can be accomplished by industry or the government acting independently. The two sides will naturally have their own perspectives on specific issues, and these may produce headlines more dramatic than the discussions warrant. But we should not allow the headlines of the day to distract us from our shared task. The government has demonstrated what sustained reform can achieve. Industry must demonstrate what sustained investment, innovation and enterprise can deliver.  Together, we must also move from ease of doing business to speed of doing business. As global supply chains are reconfigured, the time taken to approve investments, build facilities and commence production increasingly determines competitiveness. States will have a particularly important role in accelerating progress on land, power, approvals and labour.  CII intends to contribute through its councils, centres of excellence, skills initiatives and nationwide network, working with members on these six priorities and measuring progress against tangible outcomes, year after year.  The CII President writing in 2047 should be able to look back at this period as the time when the government and industry, working as Team Bharat, converted India’s economic potential into lasting prosperity.”  What that President writes then will depend on what we do now. I would like that article to be written.  
The writer is the president of CII   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. They do not necessarily reflect the opinion of www.business-standard.com or the Business Standard newspaperTopics : CII BS Opinion Development economic growth

entry.title: RBI has already answered its own listing question in case of Tata Sons
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / RBI has already answered its own listing question in case of Tata SonsRBI has already answered its own listing question in case of Tata Sons

Tata Sons met public-company standards without selling shares. The regulator's own rules show that transparency needs no listing

premium

The regulator itself admits, in writing, that listed-company transparency is possible without listing. That is where this debate belongs

Nitin Potdar5 min read Last Updated : Nov 24 2026 | 9:26 PM ISTRegulators rarely answer their own questions. However, on listing large non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) already has.  Since June 2026, an NBFC with assets of ₹1 trillion and more is regarded as an “upper layer” (RBI NBFC: Registration Directions, 2025, para 24). Further, such an NBFC “shall be mandatorily listed within three years” of being identified. And disclosures “shall be put in place on the same lines as applicable to a listed company even before the actual listing” (RBI NBFC: Governance Directions, 2025, para 43).  The RBI goes further. An unlisted upper-layer NBFC must adopt a board-approved roadmap to meet the Securities and Exchange Board of India’s (Sebi’s) listing disclosure rules (RBI NBFC Financial Statements: Directions, 2025, para 23). Even an ordinary unlisted NBFC is asked to publish a corporate governance report on the lines of Sebi’s listing obligations and disclosure requirements regulations (same directions, para 22(7)).  The regulator has said, in writing, that listed-company transparency can be achieved without listing. That is where the debate should begin.  What is left for listing to do? Is it information for the regulator?  The RBI needs no stock exchange. It can demand any statement: Capital, borrowings, investments, every borrower, every loan and its interest rate (RBI Act, s. 45L(1)(a) and (2)).  Is it for governance? The RBI already mandates audit and nomination and remuneration committees (RBI NBFC: Governance Directions, 2025, paras 17-18), a chief risk officer (paras 19), a chief compliance officer (para 25) and limits on independent directors (para 27). It also has caps on lending to any one group. None of this depends on a listing.  Listing adds nothing to how an NBFC is regulated. It changes only who owns it.  Indian company law has never equated public accountability with listing. Under the Companies Act, 1956, certain large private companies were “deemed public companies” (s. 43A). They bore the scrutiny of a public company without being made to list. Tata Sons was one of them. For years it met public-company standards; the law never asked it to sell shares to the public. It returned to private status in 2017, and the Supreme Court upheld that in 2021. Why can’t the RBI treat Tata Sons as deemed public?  RBI on listing  If listing were essential to safety, the RBI would apply it to all. It does not.  An upper-layer NBFC “fully owned and controlled by the government” is neither to list nor to make pre-listing disclosures (RBI NBFC: Governance Directions, 2025, proviso to para 43. They carry every other upper-layer obligation. Only listing is waived.  Further, certain NBFCs in a bank’s group must follow upper-layer regulations “other than the requirement of listing” (RBI NBFC: Registration Directions, 2025, para 36A, Explanation). The full rulebook, without the listing.  Most importantly, an upper-layer company can exit without ever listing: By shrinking, by a board-approved restructuring (RBI NBFC: Registration Directions, 2025, para 29), or by giving up public funds.  The risk goes. So does the listing requirement.  A safeguard that the RBI can waive, and a company can walk away from, protects no one. It is a choice of policy.  Is ownership the RBI’s business? The regulator’s power over NBFCs comes from Chapter III-B of the RBI Act, written to protect those who lend money to these companies.  Its main power covers income recognition, accounting standards, provisioning, capital adequacy, deployment of funds and lending limits (RBI Act, s. 45JA). Every item concerns the balance sheet.  The other power covers “conduct of business” (s. 45L(1)(b)): How a company lends, not who owns it. Even this requires the RBI to have “due regard to the conditions in which, and the objects for which, the institution has been established” (s. 45L(3)). One rule for every large NBFC gives no such regard.  Compare banks. When the RBI grants a private banking licence, the conditions are written in at the start: List within a set period and bring the promoters’ stake down over time. Every promoter knows this before investing a rupee. An NBFC gets no such warning. It may have been built over decades with private capital, long before any layered framework existed. Then it crosses a size threshold and is told to sell itself to the public.  A bank accepts dilution as the price of entry. An NBFC is made to pay it after the fact.  Way out and way back  There is a final irony. Listing is not even permanent. Sebi’s rules allow a listed company to delist (Sebi (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021). So, is the plan for Tata Sons to list, and then apply to delist? Why force such a somersault: Sell shares to the public, make it buy them back at a premium and put a century of philanthropy at risk on the way?  Keep everything that makes these companies safe: Capital, exposure limits, independent boards and full listed-company disclosure. Then accept that disclosure as compliance, as the Act already allows (RBI Act, s. 45NC). And treat Tata Sons as deemed public.  Globally, Denmark, Germany and Switzerland settled this long ago. Novo Nordisk, Carlsberg, Bosch and Rolex are owned or controlled by foundations, and their governments protect the model rather than question it.  Earlier this month, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman urged an amicable settlement, calling Tata group “a very critical component to the Indian economy”. An amicable settlement surely cannot mean dismantling what the nation celebrates as the Tata model.  
The writer is a senior corporate and mergers and acquisitions lawyer based in Mumbai. The views expressed are personal   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: For tariff classification, section and chapter titles have no legal force
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / For tariff classification, section and chapter titles have no legal forceFor tariff classification, section and chapter titles have no legal force

Expert answers on customs classification, FEMA reporting rules and duty-free re-export procedures for businesses

premium

Representative image for import-export

TNC Rajagopalan3 min read Last Updated : Nov 23 2026 | 11:05 PM ISTI refer to your article ‘Scotch at the Docks’, which appeared on November 16, where you have mentioned about the classification 21069051 for compound alcoholic preparations. I don’t understand why that item is under Chapter 21, which is for ‘miscellaneous edible preparations’, whereas there is a separate chapter 22 specifically for ‘beverages, spirits and vinegar’. Please clarify.  Rule 1 of the General Rules for Interpretation of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 says that “the titles of sections, chapters and sub-chapters are provided for ease of reference only; for legal purposes, classification shall be determined according to the terms of the headings and any relative section or chapter notes”. So, for classification, please do not go by the chapter or section titles only. Please go by the wording of the headings, subheadings and tariff items read with the relevant section and chapter notes and where necessary, the Interpretative Notes.   Secondly, please note that the tariff item 21069051 expressly covers qualifying ‘compound alcoholic preparations of a kind used to manufacture beverages’ and not the beverages. The distinction is between a preparation used to make a beverage and a beverage classifiable under Chapter 22.  I refer to your article ‘New FEMA rules bring small service exporters into the reporting net’ which appeared on November 4, wherein you have said that “even small service providers like individuals engaged in online teaching of music and yoga are required to furnish form EDF to the bank”. Our bankers say that it is not necessary to do so. Can you please clarify.  The position stated in my October 4, 2026 article was correct under the regulations as they stood on that date. The Reserve Bank of India subsequently amended Regulation 3(2) by a notification dated November 2, 2026, effective from October 1, 2026. Under the amended rule, a resident individual exporting services is deemed to have furnished the EDF upon giving the authorised dealer the information it requires to credit the inward re­mittance.   Your bankers are therefore right under the amended regulations. A separate EDF is unnecessary.  We had exported certain goods by claiming duty drawback and RoDTEP duty credits. Soon after exporting, we found that we had packed the goods wrongly and so, recalled the consignment for repacking and re-export. Now, we cannot use the notification 158/95-Cus dated November 14, 1995, because that is for repairs, reconditioning, reprocessing. Use of S. No.1 of notification no. 45/2017-Cus dated  June 30, 2017 would involve surrender of the export benefits and after Customs clearance and repacking, sending the goods as a fresh export claiming the benefits afresh. Is there a better way?  Yes. A warehousing route is available. File an into-bond bill of entry and move the goods to a bonded warehouse where you can ask for permission to repack the goods  for exports. After repacking, you can re-export the goods under Section 69 without payment of import duty, subject to its conditions, by filing an ex-bond shipping bill. In this route, you need not surrender any export benefits availed.

entry.title: India's mass incomes need small business growth, not just corporate jobs
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India's mass incomes need small business growth, not just corporate jobsIndia's mass incomes need small business growth, not just corporate jobs

Prime Minister's message to India Inc to practise conscious capitalism is timely, but higher corporate wages alone will not move the needle on household incomes

premium

Representative image of corporate employees at a workplace in India

Rama Bijapurkar5 min read Last Updated : Nov 23 2026 | 10:15 PM ISTThe more frequent and richer employment data being put out by the government is truly welcome. Thank you Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation for your service and looking forward to more.  It informs the discussion on how widespread the impact on household income might be were Corporate India to pay its workers more. The larger message of the Prime Minister to India Inc to practise conscious capitalism is timely and relevant, especially as there is a slippage in consumer and societal trust in big companies the world over.  However, Corporate India’s wages impact a very small sliver of Indian households and workers, and the disconnected pools of work that India has does not make for transmission of this to the many Indias that we know exist. It will, of course, create some islands or islets of increased prosperity and boost their consumption and savings, but, by and large, will not affect the earnings of the bulk of households.  Government data shows that, of about 620 million workers, about 350 million are in non-agriculture sectors, and about 280 million of them are in small, informal enterprises with fewer than 20 workers. Of the 75 million who are formally employed, it is estimated that about 30 million are employed by the government. Government data shows that about 12 per cent of employment in India’s non-farm sector is accounted for by private companies.  By way of perspective, the information technology/tech industry employs around 6 million people, and private-sector banks employ about 850,000 people. Peruse this data any which way and the conclusion is pretty much the same. What happens to formal corporate-sector wages does not directly impact most households in the country, and will not move the needle on the incomes of most households because it does not have signalling value either.  The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act set the floor for rural labour wages across the board forcing employers to match it or suffer the consequences. Government jobs, on the other hand, which pay higher salaries than private jobs have no such impact. Because of how limited these jobs are and the nature of the alternatives, young graduates, as is well known, are putting two to four years of their lives virtually on hold, or “in transit”, trying to pass competitive exams and get a well-paid government job with a predictable income. In the case of corporate jobs, even this access route does not exist.  If Corporate India were to pay its contractors more (since contract workers are the preferred option for low-skilled, labour-intensive work, in order to keep wages and headaches low), it might create some more islands of prosperity and fatten or lengthen the upper arm of the K-shaped income distribution that is so talked about nowadays. But for contractors, in turn, to share their increased income with the workers they hire is unlikely unless it is written into their contract — and it would sort of defeat the whole purpose of contracting out these activities in many cases. Minimum wage laws and better implementation are much more effective in raising worker incomes.   Eventually, higher household earnings come from increased economic activity that helps more people find more work and secure steady incomes, and from better skills that improve workers’ bargaining power and raise productivity, making employers want to pay more.  In the absence of more economic activity making better skilled jobs available, we see graduate unemployment rise and companies complain that they can’t find people for the jobs they have on offer. The push needed is to understand what it will take to get corporate India to invest big to seize the domestic market opportunity and the global opportunities that the new world is offering, with its fragmentation on one hand and the vastly improved perception — based on real demonstrated performance— of “made in India”.  As this column has often pointed out, the “no demand visibility” argument is tenuous, as is the low-capacity utilisation argument (maybe it’s the wrong kind of capacity, not producing at the price-performance point at which demand exists).  On the domestic front, the good news is that there is an even more pronounced attitude among mass-market customers of “stretch for more, not settle for less”, though the bad news is that incomes are still moving rather slowly upwards.  However, rural and urban mass-market consumers are now very similar in terms of exposure, attitudes and income, creating a mass market of enormous size. If large companies do not wish to pursue this customer, given the attractiveness of upper-income Consumer India, and if small businesses that do serve this customer currently have limits to expansion and innovation, then it is time for large companies to collect portfolios of small businesses and offer them what it will take policy a long time to do.  For large companies that have the appetite to invest in mass markets, the competitive advantage of muscle and tools (not consumer intimacy and innovation) that they could potentially have over small companies, coupled with the lack of similar sized competitors, could be a golden moment to grab. The government needs to start turbocharging its policies to help SMEs do better. For a start, detach the micro (M) from the SME and give each the tailor-made policy support that it needs.

entry.title: India's market rebound needs stronger growth to keep foreign investors
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India's market rebound needs stronger growth to keep foreign investorsIndia's market rebound needs stronger growth to keep foreign investors

Foreign investors may be back, but India cannot afford to get distracted from the growth and reform agenda

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Akash Prakash7 min read Last Updated : Nov 23 2026 | 10:07 PM ISTWhat a difference a month makes! From being ignored and at risk of irrelevance, India has come roaring back and how. In November, foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have already pumped in $13 billion and the Indian markets are up about 15 per cent in dollar terms.  Given that Korea and Taiwan are down 15-20 per cent this month, we have seen a 3000-basis-point reversal in India’s underperformance in just 20 days. Breathtaking and also scary. The North Asian breakdown has been driven by the unwinding of the artificial intelligence (AI) trade, and is global in nature. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) is down 42 per cent from its 2026 high and 25 per cent in the last month. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are down 45 per cent and 55 per cent, respectively, from their highs. The Nasdaq 100 is down 20 per cent from its high and 15 per cent in the last month. The Neoclouds have got decimated, with Coreweave down 78 per cent. FPIs are now scrambling to cover their India underweights, given the brutality and speed of the rotation away from North Asia. We see large-cap stocks in India starting to outperform.  India has benefitted from the AI selloff, but is this change in mood sustainable, or are we going to get whipsawed, with foreigners dumping the country again as soon as the AI trade is back in fashion? This is really the question. Is the change in mood on India more structural or purely tactical? How to think about this?  India is unlikely to attract the value-investor crowd. The markets are too expensive and even after 24 months of weak performance have not become cheap enough to attract the value buyer. At 18 times earnings, it is hard to call India cheap. Domestic flows, their quantum and stability, now over $50 billion per annum and growing, do not allow the markets to correct enough to become truly cheap. This dynamic is unlikely to change until such time as domestic flows reverse, which does not seem likely anytime in the near future.  So we remain a growth market. Investors come to India to buy companies that grow strongly and consistently. This is the attraction. Growth investors only care about the pace of earnings growth, its predictability and stability.  Most investors believe that India can deliver on a sustained basis 15-20 per cent earnings growth. The logic being nominal gross domestic product (GDP) grows at 12-13 per cent, the listed/organised sector grows faster and with some increase in profit share/ GDP, we can underwrite 15-20 per cent earnings growth.  There was also the belief that we can deliver this for an extended period of time and with little volatility. This was quite unique in the emerging market (EM) world. Multiples ultimately depend on earnings growth, and the predictability and stability of this growth. In a world of 3-3.5  per cent real GDP growth, 15 per cent earnings stands out. For context, the S&P 500 has delivered earnings growth at a compound annual growth rate of 7 per cent over the last 50 years. Thus, we got the valuation and attention that we did. At its peak, India accounted for over 20 per cent of the MSCI EM index and was the second-most expensive market in the world after the United States. Growth investors were all in and we had limited competition in attracting flows.  What has changed post-ChatGPT is that we are now seen as a loser of the AI buildout. If our competitive advantage of having an army of trained white-collar workers is no longer critical, is there a risk to investor growth assumptions? With our perceived weakness in innovation and the lack of cutting-edge technology, can we keep up with the anticipated surge in global productivity?  What if global investors can no longer underwrite a sustained 12-13 per cent nominal GDP growth or a non-volatile 15-20 per cent earnings trajectory? If one were to question the secular case for Indian earnings, then why pay such high multiples? Lower and more volatile growth will attract lower multiples and undermine the investment case.  What has also changed is that with the surge in AI-related capital expenditure (over $1 trillion in 2026 alone), earnings across the AI ecosystem have got supercharged. In 2026, earnings growth in the US is over 30 per cent, let alone Korea/Taiwan, which are clocking over 50 per cent. Investors believe that these elevated capex levels will continue and, therefore, so can the earnings. Again, why pay 18-20 times for India, which is growing earnings at only 15 per cent, when one can buy the US at similar multiples and Korea or the EM index at 10-12 times earnings when they are growing much faster?  With supercharged earnings across the world, the relative attractiveness of India’s 15 per cent growth has dimmed. Growth investors chasing earnings now have a choice! No one seems to care that for Korea/Taiwan or the US these are peak-of-the-cycle earnings.  For context, memory companies are currently reporting operating margins of 75 per cent. Indian earnings, not being driven by an AI buildout are not peak-of-cycle and, therefore, should be less volatile. You should obviously pay less for peak-of-cycle and highly volatile earnings as they will inevitably revert to the mean at some stage. For investors, growth is both faster and cheaper elsewhere.  India is impacted by the AI trade on two fronts, the willingness to believe in the structural nature of our growth and earnings as well as the relative attractiveness of a 15 per cent earnings trajectory.  Thus, whether the move back into India is sustained or not depends both on what we can do as a country to reinforce confidence in the India growth story, and on whether investors continue to believe in the AI buildout, its sustainability and monetisation.  The more investors believe in the structural growth of India and its earnings trajectory, the more they will be willing to pay. We need to accelerate the reforms momentum. There is genuine concern among many on India hitting a middle-income trap.  The more questions arise around the AI infrastructure buildout and its monetisation, the more investors will start normalising the supercharged current earnings of AI beneficiaries. Then, 15 per cent earnings will start looking very attractive again. India may also benefit from being seen as a beneficiary of the diffusion of AI and the broadening of use cases. The AI narrative may move away from just focusing on the infrastructure buildout.  We need both to happen for India to continue to attract foreign flows beyond the short-term catchup trade currently underway. Strengthening the case for India is the only part in our hands. We should not use the current inflows to lose focus on the steps we need to take to improve growth and productivity in India. To attract FPI capital in a sustained fashion requires the hard work of improving India’s structural growth potential. Absent that, the flows may come to hide from the current tech bloodbath but will not stay.                
 The writer is with Amansa Capital     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. They do not necessarily reflect the opinion of www.business-standard.com or the Business Standard newspaperTopics : Stock Market Foreign Portfolio Investors FPI inflows BS Opinion

entry.title: Ask businesses why they pass up export and investment opportunities
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Ask businesses why they pass up export and investment opportunitiesAsk businesses why they pass up export and investment opportunities

The government has been amending the guidelines and constituting committees to oversee implementation of the schemes

premium

Representative Picture

TNC Rajagopalan3 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 11:10 PM ISTIn February this year, the government unveiled several subsidy schemes under its Export Promotion Mission (EPM). Under some schemes, it appears, not enough exporters are coming forward to claim the subsidies. Last week, the Directorate General of Foreign Trade issued some trade notices relaxing the eligibility criteria, increasing airfare reimbursement rates and so on.  The EPM operates through two integrated sub-schemes, ‘Niryat Protsahan’, which facilitates access to trade finance, and ‘Niryat Disha’, which supports market access and addresses non-financial barriers to exports.  The six Niryat Disha interventions  are Market Access Support (MAS) to help organize/participate in trade fairs, exhibitions, buyer-seller meets and trade delegations, including airfare reimbursement for eligible participants; Trade Regulations, Accreditation and Compliance Enablement (TRACE) for partial reimbursement of eligible testing, inspection and certification costs to meet overseas requirements; Logistics Interventions for Freight and Transport (LIFT) for partial freight reimbursement for eligible micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in identified low export-intensity districts; Integrated Support for Trade Intelligence and Facilitation (INSIGHT) for supporting market intelligence, information on trade requirements and guidance to help firms identify and pursue export opportunities; Facilitating Logistics, Overseas Warehousing and Fulfilment (FLOW) for supporting access to overseas warehousing and order fulfilment infrastructure, including support for ecommerce exports; and the scheme for global outreach for branding, labelling and export packaging to help expand and sustain global markets for Indian goods and services by developing a unified brand India framework.  The government has been amending the guidelines and constituting committees to oversee implementation of the schemes.  Last Tuesday, the government enhanced the maximum eligible export turnover for availing airfare reimbursement under the MAS from ₹75 lakh in the preceding year to ₹50 crore, raised the airfare reimbursement limit up to 95 per cent for MSMEs and 80 per cent for other eligible entities, within monetary ceilings and reduced the mandatory membership period with export promotion councils from six to three months. Under the TRACE scheme, the government increased the number of testing, inspection, and certification entries eligible for reimbursement from 462 to 600.  Under the LIFT scheme, the government expanded the coverage of low export-intensity districts to 308 listed districts, expanded the categories of eligible gateways to include Land Customs Stations and Integrated Check Posts with an attached Container Freight Station, added inland waterways to the existing modes of transport, extended the air freight support for export shipments to Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, in addition to the North Eastern Region, reduced the minimum qualifying inland haul from 200 kilometre (km) to 100 km, with reimbursement limited to 400 km and extended the support to all exportable merchandise items, except those specified in the negative list of export products/categories.  It is too early to say how exporters will respond to these amendments, but one point is getting clear. The exporters will take the subsidies on offer if the activity itself, say air travel or participating in an exhibition, is justified on commercial considerations. A subsidy may tip the balance sometimes. Similarly, businesses may welcome the subsidies under the Production Linked Incentive and other schemes, income tax rate cuts, GST rate cuts, improved market access through trade agreements and so on but will invest only when it makes commercial sense.  The government should ask businesses which obstacles most often cause them to let go export or investment opportunities.

entry.title: The decade India turned the tide on poverty
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The decade India turned the tide on povertyThe decade India turned the tide on poverty

The next phase builds on this progress to lift the few people still at the bottom of the ladder out of poverty, while ensuring those who have already risen keep advancing and never slip back

Union Minister for Finance & Corporate Affairs Nirmala Sitharaman | Image: Bloomberg

Nirmala Sitharaman6 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 10:53 PM ISTA year ago, during my visit to Kiphire, an aspirational district in the remote hills of Nagaland, I interacted with tribal women from local self-help groups. Among them was Esther, a Lakhpati Didi, who proudly spoke of her millet-based products reaching customers online, far beyond Nagaland. What stayed with me was their confidence in a better future. I encouraged them to dream bigger and become Crorepati Didis. Their stories reflected a transformation reaching India's remotest corners, where geographical and economic challenges have long constrained opportunities, yet aspirations for a better tomorrow are growing. When the World Bank released its Poverty & Equity Brief on India last month, my interaction in Kiphire came back to me. The report showed that nearly 50 crore Indians had moved out of poverty between 2011 and 2023, while extreme poverty has been almost eradicated. These figures captured the transformation I had witnessed firsthand.  It was not always so. For over six decades after Independence, eradicating mass poverty remained an unfulfilled promise. Even in the early 2010s, India was portrayed abroad as a home of enduring destitution, lagging in sanitation, nutrition, clean cooking fuel and banking. The prevailing prescription was simply to put money into the hands of the poor, and poverty would take care of itself. The last decade has overturned that belief. Under PM Narendra Modi’s leadership, India has witnessed a fundamental shift from temporary relief to removing the barriers that perpetuate poverty. Guided by Antyodaya, the welfare of the last person in the line, our Government chose the harder path of addressing deprivations, household by household, ensuring development reached those who needed it most. Targeted, focused and tailored

'Kill switch': A new front in the global chip wars over tech sovereigntypremium

India can attract global capital if it removes barriers to investmentpremium

 Garibi is not merely a shortage of income or wages. A household without a secure roof, safe water, sanitation or healthcare remains vulnerable even when its income rises. One illness can wipe out savings and push a family back into poverty. Our government, therefore, made every intervention targeted at those who needed it, focused on measurable outcomes and tailored to the deprivation it was meant to remove. There was no magic wand. Each scheme required careful identification of beneficiaries, effective delivery and follow-up until the last household was reached. PM Modi has personally and painstakingly monitored implementation, intervened at critical junctures to resolve bottlenecks, ensured follow-ups and encouraged the use of technology to track delivery. This sustained attention has helped translate policy into tangible improvements in people’s lives. Health and dignity begin at home A family cannot climb out of poverty while illness and the daily burden of fetching water keep pulling it back. Under Swachh Bharat, access to household toilets has improved sanitation and helped avert an estimated 60,000-70,000 infant deaths a year. Jal Jeevan Mission has expanded rural tap-water connections from about 3 crore households in 2019 to nearly 16 crore, sparing women and girls the long walk for water and reducing exposure to waterborne diseases. Ujjwala Yojana has enabled cleaner, smokeless kitchens, while PM Awas Yojana has provided the security and dignity of pucca homes. Ayushman Bharat, offering cashless hospital care, has strengthened financial protection against medical expenses. Together, they act as insurance against the shocks that once pushed families back into poverty, while lowering household expenditure and freeing time for work. From a bank account to an enterprise Protection keeps families from slipping back into poverty; to rise further, they need opportunities to earn. For crores of people, that journey began with a bank account. Once, it was accepted that only fifteen paise of every rupee sent from the exchequer reached the intended citizen. Direct Benefit Transfer has changed that. Over 59 crore Jan Dhan accounts enable benefits to reach recipients directly, without middlemen. Technology has made this possible at an unprecedented scale. A bank account also provides a safe place for savings and helps establish a financial record, opening doors to formal credit. For those without property, access to the first loan can be life-changing. Two months ago, during an interaction with MUDRA beneficiaries, I met Sushmita Gharai from West Bengal. She lost her father during the pandemic, and her family’s printing business subsequently collapsed. With no land or gold as security, a collateral-free MUDRA loan helped her restart the press. Today, she employs 8 people, twice her initial workforce, and plans to expand into digital printing. What stayed with me was her determination to rebuild and grow. Her story reflects the aspirations of countless young Indians whose ambition exceeds their financial means. Under MUDRA, 60 crore loan accounts have been sanctioned, about two-thirds to women, while PM SVANidhi and PM Vishwakarma support street vendors and traditional artisans. Women have led this transformation. Ten crore rural women participate in SHGs that, through the DAY-NRLM and other programmes, have become platforms for savings, skills, credit and entrepreneurship. Over 3.7 crore women have become Lakhpati Didis, with some going further to become Crorepati Didis. Others, trained as Namo Drone Didis, now provide drone-spraying services to farmers. Women once excluded from economic opportunity are building enterprises and livelihoods of their own. The Sankalp for Viksit Bharat For generations, poverty was treated as something India could manage but never end. What appeared unimaginable a decade ago has now been achieved through years of steady work on the ground. Yet this is no time to rest; the road to Viksit Bharat by 2047 brings its own challenges. The next phase builds on this progress to lift the few people still at the bottom of the ladder out of poverty, while ensuring those who have already risen keep advancing and never slip back. The protection offered via various measures must now be complemented by even wider access to finance, markets and the digital economy. Government is building closer links between academia and industry through employment-linked incentives, internships and apprenticeships, while investment in infrastructure is connecting the country as never before. Opportunity cannot remain the preserve of a few.  The Prime Minister has said that Viksit Bharat, like freedom, is a commitment that every Indian must live. Having achieved in ten years what remained unfulfilled for six decades, India can face the next twenty with confidence. With the resolve of 140 crore Indians, Viksit Bharat by 2047 is within our reach, and we together will get there.
