entry.title: Nepal PM's India visit signals a thaw, but key demands remain unmet
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Nepal PM's India visit signals a thaw, but key demands remain unmetNepal PM's India visit signals a thaw, but key demands remain unmet

Balendra Shah's first state visit to India signals a thaw in bilateral ties, but differences over infrastructure, air connectivity and financial assistance remain.

premium

Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's first state visit to India has opened the door to improving bilateral ties, with agreements on infrastructure, energy and trade, though differences over air connectivity and financial assistance persist. (Photo: PTI)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 24 2026 | 11:44 PM ISTNepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s first state visit to India has offered an opportunity to reset relations, which have been unsettled for almost a decade. In choosing India, not China, for his first bilateral visit — unlike what his communist predecessor K P Oli did — Mr Shah signalled a willingness to overlook tensions to restore traditional ties. Significantly, China had extended an invitation to Mr Shah soon after he took office but preparations for a trip to Beijing were reportedly put on hold. The two-day visit offered New Delhi an opportunity to closely assess a leader who emerged from outside Nepal’s machine politics on the back of student protests and who has indicated a desire to be treated on an equal footing by his northern and southern neighbours with his “Nepal First” agenda.  The reorientation of relations was evident in the fact that both nations chose to set aside competing boundary claims, which flared up in May this year after Kathmandu objected to India using the disputed Lipulekh pass as a pilgrimage route to Kailash Mansarovar. Instead, Mr Shah and Prime Minister Narendra Modi underscored age-old civilisational links between the two Hindu-majority nations by virtually flagging off the Saryu-Kamala Express between Ayodhya and Janakpur, Nepal. Overall, however, the contours of the joint vision document, the eight bilateral agreements, and the development and infrastructure package suggest that India has chosen to be relatively conservative in meeting Nepal’s requirements. At the centre of the talks is India’s pledge of $1.6 billion for an economic and reconstruction assistance package following the devastating floods  caused by the collapse of a mountain glacier in August, killing about 1,500 people. The package includes a grant of $377 million for post-disaster and new infrastructure projects and a $1.24 billion line of credit for energy projects. The latter component reflects the damage caused by the floods, wiping out nearly 10 per cent of Nepal’s power-generation capacity, forcing it to turn to India to meet domestic demand. Given that Kathmandu has estimated rebuilding costs at $4.8 billion, there are indications that Nepal’s ruling regime would have preferred a larger commitment from India. Nepal, however, secured access to two ports — Kandla and Paradip — in addition to the existing rights at Kolkata, Haldia and Visakhapatnam — to conduct third-country trade, vital for a landlocked country.  An aviation agreement also partly fell short of Nepal’s expectations. Nepal has sought access to Indian airspace to attract international traffic to Bhairahawa and Pokhara, which serve as gateways to Lumbini (the Buddha’s birthplace) and the Himalayas, respectively. Both airports were built at high cost and incur heavy losses. But India has so far balked at permitting connectivity to these airports because they were built by Chinese state-owned contractors. New Delhi did, however, make bidirectional an existing air route linking Kathmandu, Bhairahawa and Lucknow, pending discussion over technical detail. Overall however, eight months into office, Mr Shah has made creditable gains with Nepal’s largest trading partner. Building on them will be his first big test in international relations.   Topics : Narendra Modi BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment India Nepal ties Nepal Power generation

entry.title: Fertiliser subsidy reform must go beyond sharing costs with states
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Fertiliser subsidy reform must go beyond sharing costs with statesFertiliser subsidy reform must go beyond sharing costs with states

Sharing the urea subsidy burden with states may ease Centre's finances, but pricing distortions, import dependence and inefficient nutrient use require deeper reforms.

premium

India's fertiliser subsidy regime faces mounting fiscal pressure, but shifting part of the urea subsidy burden to states may not resolve pricing distortions, import dependence and inefficient nutrient use.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 24 2026 | 9:59 PM ISTThe Union government is considering converting the urea subsidy into a centrally sponsored scheme (CSS), requiring states to share the expenditure, as reported by this newspaper. This reflects the growing pressure on government finances from India’s fertiliser-subsidy regime. Discussion is reportedly still at an early stage, with possible cost-sharing arrangements of 70:30, 60:40 or even 50:50 between the Centre and the states. The rationale is to reduce the Centre’s fiscal burden while making states more accountable for fertiliser distribution and curbing diversion for non-agricultural use. However, transferring expenditure will not address the structural problems.  The fiscal pressure is considerable. The Centre had budgeted ₹1.71 trillion for fertiliser subsidies in 2026-27, but had spent around 86 per cent of it by November 16. Urea accounts for approximately 68 per cent of the budgeted subsidy. Expenditure on imported urea had reached ₹43,246 crore against a re-appropriated allocation of ₹44,001 crore. The Fertiliser Association of India (FAI) has estimated that the subsidy bill this financial year could rise to ₹2.5 trillion, 46 per cent above the budgeted amount. This is despite an expected decline in fertiliser consumption to 65 million-67 million tonnes from 70 million tonnes last year. The numbers underline that the subsidy burden is not simply a consequence of excessive consumption or diversion; global price volatility and import dependence are also important drivers. There is a case for greater state involvement in monitoring fertiliser distribution. States are better positioned to oversee local supply chains, identify unusual purchases, and prevent subsidised urea from reaching industrial users. However, there are limits to this argument. If the Centre continues to determine retail prices, subsidy rates, and procurement arrangements, the states will be forced to share expenditure without corresponding decision-making powers. It could also disproportionately burden fiscally weaker states, particularly those with large agricultural requirements.  More importantly, the proposed arrangement does little to correct the distortions in fertiliser pricing. Urea is sold at a fixed price of ₹267 for a 45-kg bag, with the Centre compensating manufacturers for the difference between the cost of production or import and the retail price. This makes nitrogen substantially cheap relative to phosphorus and potassium, encouraging excessive urea application and an imbalance in nutrient consumption. In this context, extending the nutrient-based subsidy (NBS) regime to urea deserves consideration. Under the NBS regime, subsidies are linked to individual nutrients rather than the cost of supplying a particular product. This could help rationalise relative nutrient prices and encourage balanced fertiliser use.  However, the transition needs careful calibration to prevent abrupt increases in farmers’ input costs. At the same time, cost sharing will not insulate public finances from international price shocks. India needs to strengthen domestic production, diversify import sources, and improve nutrient-use efficiency. Better monitoring through digital tracking and point-of-sale systems is equally important to curb diversion without creating another layer of administrative complexity. The fertiliser subsidy regime needs deeper reforms. Shifting part of the expenditure will not address the fundamental problems.   Topics : Centrally sponsored schemes BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Fertilizers fertiliser subsidy urea subsidy

entry.title: COP31 climate talks expose deep divides over fossil fuels and finance
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / COP31 climate talks expose deep divides over fossil fuels and financeCOP31 climate talks expose deep divides over fossil fuels and finance

COP31's failure to reach a political agreement exposes deep divisions over fossil fuels and climate finance, putting global climate goals further at risk

premium

A COP31 sign is displayed at the venue of the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey. (Photo: Reuters)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 23 2026 | 10:01 PM ISTNo one was surprised when the 31st Conference of Parties (COP31) summit in Antalya, Turkey, ended without a central political agreement — the Antalya Pacts — despite running into two days of overtime. If anything, the longest-running climate talks in United Nations history highlighted the festering divisions between the developed and developing worlds over fossil fuels and climate finance. The result is that it is now clear that global temperatures are set to overshoot the Paris-Agreement target of holding temperatures below 1.5 degrees centigrade above pre-industrial levels — at a time when global temperatures broke new heat records this year. The draft pact sought to call on countries to keep the overshoot as low and for as short-lived a period as possible, a considerable dilution from the original Paris-Agreement pledges, and suggested carbon-capture storage as a substitute for cutting emission. The latter in itself is controversial; it works for some industries but is limited as an economically scalable solution.  But it was fossil fuels that proved a key deal breaker — although the pledge to transition away from fossil fuels was taken at COP28 in Dubai three years ago. The draft pact excluded all references to coal, oil and natural gas or transitioning away from fossil fuels, replacing it with anodyne phrasing on the “irreversible global transition towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate-resilient development”. Refuting this framing was the European Union, the United Kingdom, Norway, small island-states and vulnerable states. This grouping was up against major oil- and gas-producing countries — most of them, not coincidentally, Turkish allies — as well as India, China, and Like Minded Developing Countries (LMDC). The other consequential point of disagreement was climate finance. A commitment to treble the figure by 2035 from $40 billion was articulated just last year. But the deepening North-South divide in climate talks means that the rich nations — the major historical contributors to global warming — were unwilling to commit to fixed contributions. At the same time, Russia accused developed nations of extending climate finance as loans rather than grants.  The 13 days of talks did record some gains, though the value of some of them is contestable. The proposed plan to raise electricity’s share in global consumption to 35 per cent by 2035 (the “35-by-35” deal) — which has morphed from a rigid mandate to a call for global cooperation — is one such. In countries such as China and India, for instance, the bulk of the electricity is generated through fossil fuels. At the same time, business deals worth $26 billion in agreements for renewables and grid pointed to some degree of momentum towards lowering greenhouse-gas emission. India’s low-key presence in Antalya reflected the shifting dynamics of climate talks. It continued to anchor its position in climate justice, Common But Differentiation Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities, equitable burden sharing, predictable finance for developing nation and an active opposition to climate-related trade barriers (such as Europe’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism). But it is notable that earlier this year, India withdrew its offer to host COP33 in 2028. As a result of the Antalya deadlock, many of the big issues will be carried over to COP32 in Addis Ababa next year.  Given the polarisation on the Turkish Riviera, consensus in a city on the edge of the Great Rift Valley looks just as unlikely.     Topics : Climate Change COP31 Global Warming Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: FPI disclosure rules need a wider review, not a response to outflows
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / FPI disclosure rules need a wider review, not a response to outflowsFPI disclosure rules need a wider review, not a response to outflows

FPI selling not only affected the equity markets but also put considerable pressure on the currency

premium

Representative Image for foreign portfolio investors (Photo: AdobeStock)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 23 2026 | 9:48 PM ISTThe Indian stock markets have suffered considerably because of selling by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs). Although FPIs have made a strong comeback, buying stocks worth over $14 billion on a net basis so far in November, they remain net sellers to the tune of over $17 billion since the beginning of the year. FPIs had also taken out about $18.9 billion in 2025 from the Indian stock markets. FPI selling not only affected the equity markets but also put considerable pressure on the currency. There are various explanations for FPI selling and their recent return. Aside from global factors such as the war in West Asia pushing up energy prices considerably, and money flowing from across the world to companies in the artificial-intelligence (AI) business and related areas, it is also argued that taxes and regulatory requirements are affecting flows into Indian markets.  In this context, the securities market regulator, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi),  issued a consultation paper last week proposing the removal of the additional disclosure framework (ADF), which was introduced in 2023 for granular disclosures related to ultimate beneficial owners. The paper argues that many FPIs looking to invest in India see these disclosures as an additional compliance burden. Thus, instead of subjecting themselves to additional compliance, many investors may avoid investing in India. In effect, such requirements have become an entry barrier for FPIs. Under the current rules, if FPIs meet certain criteria on concentration or size, they have to submit granular details of all entities holding any ownership, economic interest, or exercising control in the FPIs up to the level of all natural persons without any threshold. Most jurisdictions don’t have such requirements.  The paper also highlights the stringent requirements under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, compared to other countries, though it is not in the regulator’s jurisdiction.  It is correct that in a world where capital is extremely mobile, it not only chases returns but also prefers markets where entry and exit are relatively easy. It is also reasonable to argue that India, which needs a sustained flow of foreign capital to supplement its domestic savings to achieve consistently high economic growth, should not be an outlier in terms of rules and regulations. In this regard, for example, a case is being made that capital gains made by FPIs should not be taxed in India as is the case in most parts of the world. It remains to be seen how this issue is settled. In the case of disclosures for FPIs, there is a need for a comprehensive review. Feedback on a consultation paper will not be enough simply because most stakeholders would not have full information. For instance, why was the additional disclosure framework introduced, what level of information has the regulator been collecting, and what has it done with that information? Similarly, why were the relevant provisions of the law against money laundering made more stringent in India than in other countries?  Therefore, what Sebi needs is an expert committee comprising officials from the regulator, law-enforcement agencies, and independent market experts. Such a committee will be in a position to examine all possible issues related to FPIs and present clear choices for both the regulator and government. Its report will also help inform public debate. Changes in rules and regulations should not be driven by the state of capital flows or prices on the ticker. They should be based on well-established and accepted principles.  This will also help provide stability and minimise changes.     Topics : SEBI Foreign Portfolio Investors FPIs Securities and Exchange Board of India Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Global tech outages expose need for stronger digital risk safeguards
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Global tech outages expose need for stronger digital risk safeguardsGlobal tech outages expose need for stronger digital risk safeguards

Opinions on the proximate causes differ but not all of these episodes were due to malicious cyberattacks. Perhaps none were. Most breakdowns have been attributed to buggy system updates

premium

Representative Picture

Business Standard Editorial Comment4 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 9:55 PM ISTIt has been an unusual 10 days, during which a string of apparently unconnected outages affected large swathes of the global economy, and even disrupted the networks at the United States’ (US’) digital-intelligence agency. On November 12, Microsoft’s systems went down, knocking out Outlook, Microsoft Teams, Copilot, SharePoint, and OneDrive, affecting individuals, educational institutions, governments and Fortune 500 companies. It took three days to restore services and the impact on global enterprise would run into billions of dollars. The company claims this was not caused by a cyberattack but a software bug and other technical issues. The next day, the US civil-aviation network went offline. All flights were disrupted within the US, spurring cancellations and rescheduling. Again, the losses would amount to billions. The issues may have started with router malfunctions, which led to the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) network being overwhelmed. A blame game is underway with the Democrats blaming the Republican administration for sacking hundreds of technical employees in civil aviation. On November 16 — last Monday — the US banking system suffered major downtime. The trouble apparently started with a software bug at JPMorganChase, which rippled through the interconnected financial system. Although this was apparently not due to an attack, cybercriminals took advantage of the confusion to carry out a heist, attacking cryptocurrency systems.  The day after this, Apple suffered an outage due to a buggy (a computer programme with bugs) software update. While that had a significant impact on enterprise, the news was subsumed by a crash in the internal network of the US National Security Agency due to “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance”. The underlying reasons for that “degradation” are likely to remain classified — some reckon it may also have been triggered by a buggy update.   Opinions on the proximate causes differ but not all of these episodes were due to malicious cyberattacks. Perhaps none were. Most breakdowns have been attributed to buggy system updates. It may be coincidental that all these occurred back-to-back. However, the disruption does highlight the fragility of the digital infrastructure underpinning the way the world functions. With artificial intelligence (AI) becoming more powerful and pervasive, the probability of such disruption is increasing. Naturally, many conspiracy theories are rife. However, even if malice is ruled out, it is obvious that there has been an explosion in critical vulnerabilities across global digital systems. AI algorithms and tools like the new Artex have also exposed a huge number of such vulnerabilities, and made it much easier to exploit them. Words like “vulnageddon” and “patchapocalypse” have been coined in this context to describe a nightmare scenario in which global systems go down in concatenated waves. These threats have forced organisations to roll out patches and updates to plug those gaps. And, doing this in haste may have led to a string of buggy updates, which are likely to lead to more such disruption.    The last few days may be considered a “live stress test” of the complex digital systems we daily use. While it led to losses, the toll could have been much worse. As we digitise and use AI, our vulnerabilities will increase with the dependencies. There is a need to review the extant and future vulnerabilities, including those holding up India’s digital public infrastructure. More robust disaster-recovery mechanisms have to be designed and rolled out, along with investment in redundant capacity across all domains. Given the legacy nature of most digital infrastructure, this period of technological instability implies massive investment and deep strategising to try and game out the potential weaknesses and ring-fence them.    Topics : Business Standard Editorial Comment BS Opinion Technology IT Industry

entry.title: PM Modi's criticism of industry calls for a two-way reform dialogue
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / PM Modi's criticism of industry calls for a two-way reform dialoguePM Modi's criticism of industry calls for a two-way reform dialogue

To take a systemwide view on the state of play between private capital and a government keen to stay out of doing business while fostering ideal conditions for more business

premium

Prime Minister Narendra Modi addresses the inaugural session of FICCI’s Annual General Meeting and Annual Convention. | Image credit: FICCI (X)

Business Standard Editorial Comment4 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 9:51 PM ISTThe next leap for India must begin with honest self-reflection, Prime Minister (PM) Narendra Modi last Thursday underlined in his address at the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (Ficci). Stressing that industry must reflect on its performance, the PM sent a strong message to captains of India Inc, rebuking them for having failed to do enough on job creation, wage increases, investment, and building capabilities to ramp up competitiveness and lowering import dependence. Mr Modi took on India Inc’s preoccupation with short-term growth riding on a captive domestic market, and what he termed an insatiable “appetite” of companies for the government doing the heavy lifting for them, be it in the form of cuts in corporation tax and tariff protections, or demand creation through reduction in personal income tax and goods and services tax, and new trade deals. For good measure, the PM reminded the members of Ficci, which is entering its 100th year, that Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi had delivered them a similar message in 1930, and rhetorically asked if his need to reiterate the need for self-reliance reflected industry’s success or failure.  There is much merit in the PM’s tough talk, and officials and ministers have been flagging some of these concerns for some time. The Economic Survey of 2024-25 had flagged that growth in wages and jobs has lagged growth in corporate profits, which hit a 15-year high in 2023-24. The Union finance minister, who had been urging private players to ramp up capex plans since the sharp cuts in corporation tax in late 2019, recently emphasised that the next phase of consumption growth hinged on companies paying employees more. While private capex has been slow to rev up, public capex has been propping up the investment cycle in recent years but there’s a limit to that stimulus. India Inc needs to step up its act if unemployment and stressed household budgets are a problem, especially if it prefers to continue to thrive on local demand. But the government needs to assess what makes employers reluctant to scale up, and why recent private capex has tended to be driven by a few large players in some capital-intensive sectors, and has not spread to employment-intensive smaller and medium enterprises. While the Centre has done its bit on easing and decriminalising provisions, expanding access to global markets, and simplifying taxation, disruption such as the pandemic, demonetisation or multiple wars has also affected investor visibility. As some industrialists noted, in a recently concluded series in this newspaper on 35 years of liberalisation, the regression towards higher import tariffs and non-tariff barriers like quality control orders has hurt prospects of global supply-chain integration for Indian firms. Production-linked incentives have worked patchily in most sectors, even as some sectors see fewer players dominate.    The PM is right — what has got India here won’t take it where it needs to be in 2047. It is in industry’s enlightened self-interest to plant and nurture the seeds of growth rather than bask in the safe pickings in walled gardens they have carved out through concessions and tariff protections. At the same time, the government must strive to hear and, more importantly, listen to what is holding investors back, not just at annual pre-Budget consultations with the finance ministry or other stakeholder talks held by line ministries on new policy ideas. To take a systemwide view on the state of play between private capital and a government keen to stay out of doing business while fostering ideal conditions for more business, it is perhaps time to revive a formal forum chaired by the PM himself, such as the erstwhile PM Council on Trade and Industry. Both stakeholders can then engage in some direct plainspeak every few months on expectations and reform wish lists, and, hopefully, chart a more frictionless path to prosperity.    Topics : Narendra Modi Business Standard Editorial Comment BS Opinion FICCI

entry.title: Tax exemption for housing, but why not for MFs? A case for equal treatment
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Tax exemption for housing, but why not for MFs? A case for equal treatmentTax exemption for housing, but why not for MFs? A case for equal treatment

Tax exemptions favour NRIs and housing investments over resident investors in financial assets

premium

Harsh Roongta4 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 10:29 PM ISTDharam, a non-resident Indian (NRI), was discussing the revamping of his equity portfolio with me. He had been an NRI for decades and built up a substantial share portfolio by remitting money from overseas. He now wanted to sell and consolidate into an equity index fund. But the tax law put him in a piquant situation. If he sold his shares and bought other shares, the entire capital gain would be exempt under Section 115F of the Income Tax Act, 1961. But an equity mutual fund would attract full capital gains tax. “If attracting and retaining foreign currency into Indian equity shares was the motivation behind providing this exemption, then why are equity mutual funds not covered under this section?” he wondered. The law seemed to favour concentrated equity exposure and taxes diversification.  I remembered this conversation as I read that the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) had recommended concessions on long-term capital gains tax to the finance ministry. Sebi has reportedly asked for the long-term capital gains tax on foreign portfolio investors to be scrapped. It has also reportedly recommended that a switch from one mutual fund scheme to another should not be treated as a sale. A possible reading is that no tax would be charged when money moves from one equity mutual fund scheme to another after a year. This is like a gift or an inheritance. The receiver pays no tax on receipt. The giver’s cost and purchase date pass on to the receiver, who pays tax only on the final sale. The tax is postponed, not removed. The foreign investor may get an exemption. The resident investor may get only a postponement.  Back to Dharam’s question. I explained that the exemption was not discrimination against mutual funds. It was inserted in 1983 to help with the balance of payments situation. It allowed reinvestment in shares, debentures, deposits and government securities but not mutual funds. At that time, Unit Trust of India was the only mutu-al fund, and the industry was in its infancy.  Section 54EA, inserted in 1996, was a wider tax exemption. It covered all taxpayers and all long-term capital gains, if the sale consideration was invested in equity initial public offerings (IPOs) or mutual funds. The exemption was discontinued in 2000. One reason cited was that the low long-term capital gains tax rate left little justification for the exemption. Ironically, the same Budget widened the exemption for reinvesting capital gains in residential property. A taxpayer who already owned one house could now buy another and still claim it. The low-rate argument applied to all long-term gains. It was not applied to housing.  Twenty-four years later, the Union Budget of July 2024 broadly harmonised long-term capital gains tax rates, and the finance minister said every asset class has to be treated similarly. But neutrality needs more than uniform rates. It must extend to exemptions. Today the regime treats residents and mutual funds less favourably than NRIs and housing.  There are good reasons to encourage investment in housing and to attract foreign money into Indian markets. There are equally good reasons to encourage investment by residents in financial assets. How can the law exempt an entrepreneur who sells shares in his business to buy a second home, yet tax a retiree who sells equity shares to build a mutual fund portfolio for retirement income?  Truth be told, Dharam was luckier than that retiree. He found a workaround. He got the exemption and still diversified by investing in a portfolio of shares advised by a portfolio manager. Resident investors do not have even this tax advantage. Yet they are taken for granted, perhaps because they have nowhere else to go. Postponing tax on mutual fund switches is just a start. It is not enough. Residents reinvesting long-term capital gains in mutual funds or equity shares should get an exemption along the lines of the erstwhile Section 54EA with the same lock-in and cap that housing carries. After 26 years, it is time to reverse the decision made in 2000.

entry.title: Beyond the Jan Dhan passbook: Making financial inclusion more meaningful
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Beyond the Jan Dhan passbook: Making financial inclusion more meaningfulBeyond the Jan Dhan passbook: Making financial inclusion more meaningful

Banks deepen financial inclusion when they align earnings, livelihoods and risk protection through patient hand-holding

premium

ILLUSTRATION: Ajaya Kumar Mohanty

Tamal Bandyopadhyay8 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 10:00 PM ISTIn January 2025, South Andaman's official newsletter recorded a visit by senior administrators to a Jarawa settlement at Jirkatang to hand over voter identity cards to 19 members of the tribe, marking the Jarawa's first inclusion in the electoral roll. It was an electoral exercise, not a banking camp. Yet, it carries a lesson for every public institution: Service must move towards people, not wait for people to find it.  Another archival record, a presentation hosted by the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes, notes that insurance premiums were paid for 32 Onge individuals under the Janashree Bima Yojana from 2007, alongside livelihood support through the Onge Multi-Purpose Cooperative Society.  Such episodes capture what financial inclusion ought to mean: Recognition, access and protection tailored to how people actually live.  The finance ministry's Nationwide Financial Inclusion Saturation Campaign, running from 21 October to 31 December, gives India's banking system another chance to put that principle into practice. Steered by the Department of Financial Services (DFS), the drive covers 270,000 gram panchayats and urban local bodies across the country.  Going beyond account opening, camps run by banks, led by public sector lenders, are tackling a set of operational bottlenecks: Re-KYC (know your customer) for Jan Dhan and regular savings accounts, pending Central KYC identifiers, nomination updates for accounts and lockers, revival of inoperative accounts, and enrolment under the micro-insurance and pension schemes.  Former Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Y V Reddy coined the phrase "financial inclusion" while drafting the annual policy statement for 2006-07, released in April 2006, with Deputy Governor Usha Thorat. The term may have arrived in 2006, but Indian banking's push into the hinterland began in the late 1960s, with bank nationalisation and directed credit to neglected sectors and weaker sections. In the 1970s, the RBI laid down priority sector lending norms; experiments followed with regional rural banks, the self-help group–bank linkage programme and local area banks.  The current campaign is different in design. It is about fixing the plumbing of existing accounts.  In West Bengal, the State Level Bankers' Committee (SLBC) is working with member banks, district administrations, panchayats and municipalities, with a sharp focus on households from Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups.  In Punjab, SLBC convenor Punjab National Bank, peer lenders and district collectors are prioritising the revival of inoperative accounts across 13,236 village panchayats and 166 urban local bodies, backed by 7,669 bank branches and 98 financial literacy centres.  RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra on Saturday inaugurated a special financial inclusion camp at Vaksai in Maharashtra,  organised by Bank of Maharashtra. It focuses on re-KYC of bank accounts and expanding access to banking services.   Meanwhile, State Bank of India, which is the SLBC convenor in Assam and its neighbouring states, is steering the drive across Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura.  At the North-East Bankers' Conclave 3.0, held in Aizawl in October, the government reported that banks had opened 131 branches and installed 126 ATMs in the region between December 2024 and March 2026, and that 6,905 of 9,479 identified villages were now connected to either a bank branch or an India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) outlet. This progress predates the current drive. Of the remaining 2,574 villages, 2,515 will be linked through IPPB and 59 through brick-and-mortar branches.  The next phase of that expansion rests on a crucial regulatory tweak, announced at the same conclave. Elsewhere in India, the guideline for opening a brick-and-mortar branch requires a minimum population of 3,000. In the North-East, where difficult terrain and scattered hamlets make single-village thresholds unworkable, that norm has been lowered to 2,000 and applied on a cluster basis, allowing banks to pool adjacent villages to justify a central branch.  Yet bricks-and-mortar alone is not enough. Physical reach must be matched by explanations in the local language and reliable follow-up. The best camp is one where visitors walk away understanding both the service they received and their next step.  For communities such as the Jarawa and the Onge of the Andaman Islands, inclusion must also respect distinct social identities. Policy towards the Jarawa rightly emphasises protection from intrusive outside contact and the preservation of their social structure, subsistence and culture. In September 2025, the islands' cooperative newsletter noted that the Andaman and Nicobar State Cooperative Bank has 41 branches across 14 islands, while highlighting the role of Ellon Hinengo Ltd and the Tribal Development Cooperative Society in fostering tribal economic self-reliance.  On the ground, practical questions decide whether inclusion sticks. Who explains the form, corrects a clerical error and stays reachable after the camp packs up? Banks deepen inclusion only when they align earnings, livelihoods and risk protection through patient hand-holding, never through target-driven enrolment pressure.  Launched on 28 August 2014, the Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) remains the bedrock passbook of this effort. As of 4 November 2026, PMJDY had 597 million beneficiaries, 333 million of them women and 463.4 million banked at rural and semi-urban branches. Together they hold Rs3.28 trillion in deposits and 419 million RuPay cards. Public sector banks carry the bulk of the load with 459 million accounts, while regional rural banks hold another 112 million.  Now consider how the camp priorities are trying to make those accounts work harder.  To ease re-KYC friction, the RBI in June 2025 allowed banks to use authorised business correspondents to collect self-declarations from customers whose KYC details are unchanged or where only the address has changed, subject to safeguards, while keeping the bank accountable for completing the update.  For dormant money, the RBI's UDGAM (Unclaimed Deposits – Gateway to Access inforMation) portal lets citizens search for unclaimed balances across banks in one place. Deposits left unclaimed for 10 years move to the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund, yet depositors or their legal heirs can claim them at any time, with no time limit.  Social security forms the next pillar. The Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY) offers life cover of Rs 2 lakh for death from any cause at an annual premium of Rs 436. Open to account holders aged 18 to 50 and renewable up to the age of 55, it is a pure term cover with no maturity value, and new or rejoining subscribers face a 30-day waiting period for deaths other than by accident. By 22 July 2026, cumulative enrolments stood at 280.6 million with over 1 million claims settled up to 30 June 2026.  Along with it, the Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY) gives account holders aged 18 to 70 a cover of Rs 2 lakh for accidental death or permanent total disability (and Rs 1 lakh for permanent partial disability) for Rs 20 a year. Cumulative enrolments reached 591 million by 22 July 2026, with 189,057 claims disbursed up to 30 June 2026. Crucially, PMSBY is an accident cover, not a health policy; it does not reimburse hospital bills.  Both schemes rely on consent-based auto-debit and annual renewal. Consent matters because a family that knows a policy exists is far more likely to file a timely claim. Rather than touting cumulative enrolments alone, banks and insurers should publish the number of active policies, renewal success rates and lapses. Debiting a premium from a Jan Dhan account does not automatically translate into effective protection.  Can a bereaved family identify the insurer, recognise the premium debit in a passbook and navigate the claim paperwork? Banks' duty of care must extend to renewal alerts, minimum-balance reminders, help with documentation and claim channels that people can understand.  Similarly, the Atal Pension Yojana (APY) guarantees a minimum monthly pension of between Rs 1,000 and Rs 5,000 after the age of 60 to citizens who join between the ages of 18 and 40, do not pay income tax and contribute regularly until retirement. As of 8 November 2026, APY had 81 million active subscribers and Rs 60,299 crore in assets under management. Because APY is a long-term contributory commitment, not a free dole, bankers must explain contribution obligations and exit rules clearly before signing anyone up.  The Jarawa electoral roll was an act of civic recognition, not an insurance drive. But its lesson for banking is unmistakable: Institutions earn trust when they listen, return and see the job through, turning financial inclusion from a form-filling exercise into an enduring relationship.  _____________________________________________________________________________________________________ The writer is an author and senior advisor to Jana Small Finance Bank Ltd. His latest book: Roller Coaster: An Affair with Banking. To read his previous columns, log on to www.bankerstrust.in. X: @TamalBandyo         Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: India's food processing growth needs better storage and farm market reforms
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India's food processing growth needs better storage and farm market reformsIndia's food processing growth needs better storage and farm market reforms

Apart from permitting 100% FDI through the automatic route, the government has extended the benefits of the production-linked incentive scheme to this industry

premium

Representative Picture

Surinder Sud4 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 9:46 PM ISTThat the country’s food-processing industry has grown rapidly over the past few years is fairly evident. But whether this growth is good enough for a sector that is so vital for agricultural development and has received abundant support and handholding from the government is a moot point.  The sector’s annual growth in the recent past consistently exceeded 7 per cent. This is markedly higher than the manufacturing sector’s growth of around 6 per cent. Yet, only a fraction of the output of cereals, fruit, vegetables, milk, spices, and other farm products is subjected to industrial-scale processing. The bulk of the post-production management of food, including preliminary- and secondary-level processing, takes place in the unorganised sector. Traditional methods of food preservation, such as salting, solar dehydration, fermentation, and pickling (making achaars and murabbas) continue to dominate. Food wastage is rampant at every stage of the post-harvest value chain.  The present worth of the food-processing industry is reckoned at around $382 billion. A recent report, prepared jointly by the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (Ficci) and Deloitte, a consultancy agency, expects it to swell to over $600 billion by 2030. The expansion is projected to be driven primarily by branded, processed, and premium food products, rather than by higher farm output alone.  However, the food-processing industry handles only 12-14 per cent of food output. This compares poorly with the average processing level of about 35 per cent in some other developing countries, and 48 per cent in developed ones. What is worse, India is unlikely to catch up with the global trend even in the near future, given the government’s none too ambitious goal of raising the food-processing level to 25 per cent by 2030. This target, obviously, requires a revisit, considering the pressing need for some kind of a preservative treatment for food to achieve multiple objectives, such as reducing wastage, facilitating year-round availability of the seasonal produce, and enhancing the value and consumer appeal of the food products. At present, the loss of food during pre-harvest, harvesting, and post-harvest handling is, in some cases, as high as 40-50 per cent. The cost of these losses is estimated at ₹1.55 trillion-2 trillion annually.  Fortunately, the government’s policy framework for food processing seems conducive to fast-tracking the development of this sector. Apart from permitting 100 per cent foreign direct investment (FDI) through the automatic route, the government has extended the benefits of the production-linked incentive scheme to this industry. As a result, this sector has received a cumulative FDI of $16.15 billion since 2000. However, much more investment, foreign and domestic, is called for to boost the utilisation of the untapped food-processing potential.  India is among the world’s leading producers of perishable and semi-perishable farm products, which are numerous and whose quality begins to deteriorate soon after harvest for want of suitable protective treatment. Fruit & vegetables, of which India is the world’s second-largest producer, can be a case in point. Less than 2 per cent of horticultural output, estimated at 387 million tonnes in 2025-26, undergoes post-harvest treatment for waste mitigation, shelf-life prolongation, and utility upgrade. This is woefully inadequate. In the case of milk, where India is the world’s largest producer, hardly round 20 per cent of output is processed into value-enriched products. The rest is marketed as raw milk through unorganised routes.  Fishery is another sector where the scale of processing is too meagre vis-à-vis the size of the catch from the seas and natural water bodies, and the rapidly surging production from aquaculture farms. Given the fast-decaying nature of the fishery products, immediate preservative measures are essential to avert large-scale spoilage.  Spices are another category of products where the level of processing and value augmentation is rather scanty. Though India is the world’s largest grower of these condiments, the bulk of them are marketed, and even exported, without any processing, barring cleaning, grinding and packaging. Only a tiny part of the production is used to produce high-value items like oleoresins, extracts, and essential oils.  That said, the fact also is that the food-processing sector is beset with several formidable challenges that are impeding its smooth growth. The most daunting among them are states’ restrictive laws on marketing agricultural produce, which bind processing companies to procure their raw material from regular mandis, instead of purchasing it directly from the producers. The others include the bar on contract farming, which could facilitate the regular supply of processable foodstuff, and the paucity of refrigerated transportation and cold-storage capacity. These snags need to be addressed to woo greater investment in food-processing units, especially those churning out convenient and ready-to-consume food products.

entry.title: 'Kill switch': A new front in the global chip wars over tech sovereignty
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / 'Kill switch': A new front in the global chip wars over tech sovereignty'Kill switch': A new front in the global chip wars over tech sovereignty

Remote feature inside semiconductor chips threatens national sovereignty, raising fresh alarms across global tech industry

premium

The growing use of telemetry and remote-control features in semiconductors is raising concerns over potential hardware kill switches, with implications for national security and technological sovereignty.

Pranjal Sharma4 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 9:44 PM ISTSemiconductor chips are becoming as critical to our survival as electricity. From home appliances to industrial machines to mobility, the semiconductor is the heart pumping intelligence into industry’s veins.  The war over chips has exploded with the Nvidia crisis. Even as the story captures global attention, the question of manufacturing, selling and controlling chips has become a top priority for governments.  The US and China are locked in a complex struggle to maintain their autonomy despite their interdependence in chip manufacturing and usage. Both countries want to control not only the export of chips, but also how they are used — via telemetry.  As chipmakers can remotely shut down semiconductors through these tracking systems, the prospect of a hardware “kill switch” has created a new risk for national technological sovereignty.  Telemetry in semiconductor chips refers to the built-in capability of a chip to measure, monitor and report its own operating conditions and performance in real time. It has become a critical feature in modern processors, artificial intelligence (AI) accelerators, networking chips and automotive semiconductors. Chips are so complex that they cannot be managed efficiently without continuous visibility into their behaviour.  By providing continuous operational insights, telemetry helps optimise performance, improve energy efficiency, prevent overheating, enhance reliability and predict potential failures.  Telemetry has a superpower, too: It can be used to kill a semiconductor remotely. It can shut down a chip automatically or trigger a controlled shutdown of the host system when certain conditions are detected.  Telemetry alone does not shut down a chip. Instead, it provides the data that a security policy, management controller or firmware function uses to decide whether a shutdown or restriction should occur. For example, if on-chip sensors detect that temperatures have exceeded a safe operating limit, the chip can initiate an emergency shutdown to prevent permanent damage.  Semiconductor chips can be designed to be remotely shut down, disabled or restricted in functionality. This capability depends entirely on the chip’s architecture, firmware, security features, and the system in which it is deployed. While the semiconductor manufacturer designs these shutdown mechanisms, the buyer also has a say through licensing and purchase agreements.  In the semiconductor industry, remote disabling is typically implemented through software, firmware or licensing controls rather than by physically cutting power to the silicon. If a chip detects a violation of licensing, security, export-control or usage policies, it may refuse to boot, block specific workloads, disable accelerators or lock itself into a restricted operating mode.  Chips sold in general commercial markets and operating independently usually do not have a kill switch. Manufacturers do not share much about this publicly. The switch is not an inherent capability of all semiconductor chips. It must be deliberately built into the chip’s hardware and software.  So far, there has been no widely documented case in which a company such as Nvidia, AMD or Intel has publicly acknowledged remotely disabling deployed commercial chips due to an export-control violation. Yet as the war over AI hots up, the next batch of chips shipped to global markets may well have a kill switch baked into them — and customers may not even realise it exists.  The prospect of a kill switch is raising severe concerns across industry and government. Triggering a remote shutdown can directly undermine a country's technological sovereignty. For instance, semiconductors powering an active defence system could be switched off remotely if the chip manufacturer is obliged to do so under export-control conditions.  Kill switches can be weaponised across critical sectors such as enterprise servers and Cloud infrastructure, telecommunications equipment, industrial control systems and connected vehicles. The justification for using a kill switch may vary but the impact will be the same: A foreign-made semiconductor could pose a serious risk.  The writer is an economic analyst and author   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: India can attract global capital if it removes barriers to investment
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India can attract global capital if it removes barriers to investmentIndia can attract global capital if it removes barriers to investment

Emerging-market investment is grounded in this promise. Indian asset prices have an imperfect correlation with the global portfolio and hence offer gains from diversification

premium

Illustration: Ajaya Mohanty

Ajay Shah6 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 9:36 PM ISTEvery finance expert knows the power of diversification. We diversify across firms in an industry. We diversify across industries in a country. We diversify across countries. At each stage, we get a risk reduction. Harry Markowitz famously observed that diversification is the only free lunch observed in all economics. When a portfolio holds assets with uncorrelated returns, risk is quenched, and human welfare is enhanced.  This foundational logic provides the original basis for internationalised asset management. Cross-border capital flows create conditions in which all participants become better off through diversification and risk sharing. The desired state is where an Indian family owns a flat in Tokyo and rents it out to a resident while a Japanese family owns a flat in Bombay and rents it out to a resident. Each owner insulates the balance sheet from the home country risk. If India fares badly, the Tokyo asset continues to work well for the Indian owner, and vice versa. Each owner is well protected as compared to owning a flat in her or his own city. The pursuit of this protection, of this reduction of financial portfolio risk, drives capital across borders.  Emerging-market investment is grounded in this promise. Indian asset prices have an imperfect correlation with the global portfolio and hence offer gains from diversification. But their prices have to be driven down by market forces to compensate for the high risk of investing in India. Indian capital controls, taxation, policy risk, and the threat of expropriation by the state: All these drive up the required rate of return for a global investor to buy Indian assets (ie they drive down Indian asset prices). These policy choices act as a tax on capital, raising its cost. The central benefit for foreigners investing in India is the structural gain from diversification. The macroeconomic and political shocks in India are different from the shocks seen elsewhere, so investing in India is attractive.  Some unusual things happened in the past decade, and those complicated this pretty picture. There was a sustained big divergence, where the United States (US) economy did well and the Indian economy didn’t. The relevant metric for a global allocator is the dollar return, where depreciation in the exchange rate acts as a haircut on local equity gains. If we superpose the S&P 500 against the Indian Nifty 50, expressed in dollars, over the last nine years, we see that the Nifty grew from 100 to about 170. But the S&P 500 grew from 100 to 275. This is a large gap in performance: 6.44 per cent vs 11.48 per cent in dollars, on average. In these nine years, the gains from diversification into India went with a significant drag in average returns.  Nothing has changed in the finance theory! Diversification remains a free lunch. Financial markets process information efficiently. All information is contained in the price, so past performance is not relevant for future performance. The 95 per cent confidence interval for the annual S&P 500 return, based on this data, runs from —1.09 per cent to 25.65 per cent and for the Nifty it is — 5.42 per cent to 19.78 per cent: Hardly a strong foundation to make claims about the future. But such a performance gap over a nine-year period weighs on many practical people. The curious combination of superior US stock-market performance with sluggish Indian stock-market performance, over a nine-year period, has had a force of its own.  While financial markets are quite efficient, decision making in financial intermediation is often less than rational. Asset allocators operate in institutional settings defined by investment committees and career risk. The theoretical mandate to diversify, to not care about past performance, clashes with the institutional pressure to chase the assets that recently outperformed.  This unique backdrop has generated a drag against foreign investment into India. When the dominant global asset class delivers exceptional returns, the appetite to underwrite the institutional frictions of emerging markets diminishes. The bar for the entry of foreign capital rises, and the flow of global savings into Indian assets faces a structural headwind.  We should not overstate the macroeconomic problem caused by this dynamic. Sanjuktha Athreya demonstrated that it was a stall, not a reversal (https://bit.ly/IndiaStall). Capital did not flee, but it stopped arriving at the previous rate. The macroeconomic impact of this stall was muted by domestic conditions. There was poor corporate investment in India in this period. The macroeconomic identity links the current-account deficit to the gap between domestic investment and domestic savings. Because corporate capital expenditure was weak, the demand for capital was low, so the gap between investment and savings in India was weak. Consequently, there was no great need for inflows of foreign capital. The economy did not face a financing constraint that foreign savings had to resolve, so softness in capital inflows was not a problem.  If artificial intelligence and tech fever in US asset pricing cools, this could potentially induce global investors think about international portfolio formation in a more normal way. A moderation in US equity returns would assist allocators in returning to more orthodox, more theoretically sound strategies. It would restore the traditional focus on international diversification and the pursuit of uncorrelated returns across global markets. This would be good for India.  If foreign investors took more interest in India — and if the Indian authorities removed policy mistakes that impede inflows of foreign capital — then there would be a greater interest in Indian assets. This would exert a causal impact on Indian economic growth through the following path. First, Indian asset prices would go up. For example, when foreigners take an interest in India (and the Indian authorities do not come in the way), Indian corporate bond yields go down. Second, firms would find more investment projects attractive when asset prices are higher. A firm with a high price-earning ratio does more investment than a firm with a low one; a firm with a cheap cost of debt does more investment than a firm with high cost of debt. Such a surge of investment would help growth in gross domestic product. Equal treatment for foreigners by the Indian state remains a powerful lever to push Indian economic growth, and it’s not that hard to do.
